title: A Statistical Learning Perspective on Semi-dual Adversarial Neural Optimal Transport Solvers
one_liner: The paper proves that neural networks solving transport problems via adversarial games learn a correct solution from finite data, not just luck.
lead: Imagine you have two piles of stuff and want to rearrange one pile to match the other in the most efficient way. A neural network can learn this rearrangement by playing a game: one network proposes moves, another network critiques them, and together they figure out the optimal plan. But no one knew whether this game actually teaches the network the right solution or just makes it memorize the training data—because networks can fit any data perfectly if given enough parameters, whether or not they understand the pattern. This paper proves that the game teaches the network the underlying solution, as long as you collect enough training data.

problem.h2: The unsolved mystery: does the game teach or just memorize?
paras: Neural networks are good at finding patterns in data. But when a network learns by playing a two-player game, it is not obvious that what it learns will work on new, unseen data. A beginner might assume that if the game feels like it is working (the players keep adjusting their moves), the network has truly figured out the transport problem. But the network could simply be memorizing the exact training examples, with no real understanding. When you hand it a new rearrangement task it has never seen, it fails completely.

Researchers built neural networks that solve optimal transport (the rearrangement problem) by having two networks compete: one tries to move stuff, the other judges whether the moves are good. The method works in practice on real tasks like translating images or making them sharper. But the theory was silent: no one had proven that networks trained this way actually learn the underlying pattern, not just the training data. There was no guarantee.

callout.html: When networks learn via adversarial games, the network that proposes solutions actually learns to solve the real problem, not just memorize training examples.

object.h2: What the paper changes: the generalization guarantee
paras: The paper adds something that did not exist before: a mathematical proof that the mover network—the one that proposes the rearrangement solution—actually learns the right mapping, not just memorizes. In technical terms, it bounds how far the learned mapping can drift from the true optimal transport map.

hidden.name: generalization gap
paras: The generalization gap is the difference between how well the mover performs on training data (the examples you showed it) and how well it performs on brand-new data it has never seen. If a network memorizes training data, the gap is huge: it is perfect on the examples but fails on new ones. If it truly learned the pattern, the gap is tiny: it is almost as good on new data as on training data.

The paper estimates this gap using two ingredients: how complicated the network is (its functional class size) and how many training samples you provide. The idea is borrowed from classical statistics: the more samples you have and the simpler your model, the smaller the gap tends to be. The paper formalizes this for optimal transport networks.

heat.caption: Hotter weights have bigger gaps; training tightens gaps over all weights.

Generalization error is bounded by sample size and network complexity.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the argument is purely statistical
paras: Optimal transport adversarial training is a form of supervised learning in disguise. The judge network never appears in the final guarantee—only the mover matters. The mover is learning a function from source data to target data. Classic statistical learning theory says: if you train a function on many random samples, the function will generalize (work on new data) as long as two things hold: (1) the function class is not too complicated, and (2) you have enough samples. The paper shows that optimal transport networks satisfy both conditions. The complexity grows with network width and depth, but standard mathematical properties of neural nets bound it. The number of samples needed is determined by how accurately you want to solve the transport problem—tighter solutions require more data, which makes sense.

Why does the adversarial game part not wreck this? Because even though the judge network changes during training, the mover is always solving the same underlying problem: learn to move stuff in a way that fools the judge. If the judge is imperfect (which it is, initially), the mover learns a slightly imperfect solution—but the gap shrinks as both train. The paper shows that the mover's generalization gap depends only on the mover's complexity, not the judge's, and that gap closes with more data. The game itself is a training mechanism; the learning is still fundamentally supervised.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose Complexity(F) = 400 and n = 100 training pairs.
Then E_gap <= sqrt(400 / 100) = sqrt(4) = 2 percentage points.
With n = 400 pairs, E_gap <= sqrt(400 / 400) = 1 percentage point.
With n = 1600 pairs, E_gap <= sqrt(400 / 1600) = 0.5 percentage point.
Doubling sample size shrinks error by a factor of sqrt(2), making the guarantee tighter.

math.note: The bound says: train on enough data (sample size) and use a simple model (low complexity), and the mover will transfer to new rearrangement problems.

items.html: If the mover network has millions of parameters and you only train on 10 examples, the bound is loose—it says the gap could be huge. The theory still holds but does not tell you the network will work.
If the judge is bad at scoring, the mover only learns an approximate solution. The paper bounds the final error but assumes the judge is minimally competent.
If the true optimal transport map is very wiggly (requires a huge network to represent), you need exponentially more data. The bound grows with complexity, so hard problems demand more samples.
The guarantee is an upper bound—it may be much tighter in practice than the formula predicts. The paper does not tighten it per se, but it does prove generalization is guaranteed.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple toy transport problem: move points from one 2D cluster to another. Train the mover and judge networks on 100 random training pairs. Measure accuracy on the training set and on a separate test set of 50 new pairs. Repeat with 200, 500, and 1000 training samples. Plot training accuracy (should stay high) and test accuracy (should grow toward training accuracy). Show that the generalization gap shrinks as sample size grows, matching the prediction: gap shrinks as one over square root of sample size. Verify that test accuracy approaches training accuracy, proving the network learned the pattern, not memorized the data.
demo.closing: The gap must shrink as you add more training data, proving the network generalized, not memorized.
